lead: Ben Sira warns against false confidence: trust in wealth, trust in one’s own strength, and trust that mercy can be put off until later. In the Gospel Jesus speaks just as plainly: a cup of water given to his disciples will be rewarded, and whatever leads us or others into sin must be cut away. Psalm 1 sets the two ways side by side, the tree planted by streams of water and the chaff that the wind drives away.

r.h: Do not delay to turn back to the Lord
set: After his chapters on wisdom and humility, Ben Sira gives a string of short commands, nearly all beginning “Do not”. Each warns against a confidence that is false: in money, in one’s own strength, in God’s patience, in God’s mercy taken for granted.

Ben Sira writes before the clear revelation of the life to come. When he speaks of punishment and of the day of calamity, he thinks first of judgment within this life. Later revelation opens the fuller horizon, but his call to conversion stands.
str: vv. 1–2: do not trust wealth or your own strength.
vv. 3–4: do not say that no one can call you to account.
vv. 5–6: do not presume on forgiveness.
vv. 7–8: turn back today; dishonest wealth will not save you.
kw: The Greek word behind “turn back” (v. 7) is the Bible’s great word for conversion: to turn around and come home to God.
God’s patience (v. 4) is real, but it is given so that we may repent, not so that we may go on sinning. Paul says the same in Romans 2:4.
“Both mercy and wrath are with him” (v. 6). Ben Sira does not deny mercy; he warns against using it as an excuse.
vv: Do not say, “I sinned, yet what has happened to me?” for the Lord is slow to anger.
Because nothing happened at once, the sinner thinks nothing will happen. God’s delay is not approval; it is an invitation.
Do not be so confident of forgiveness that you add sin to sin.
This is presumption: counting on forgiveness while refusing conversion.
Do not delay to turn back to the Lord, and do not postpone it from day to day;
St Augustine remembered how, before his conversion, he kept saying “tomorrow, tomorrow” (Confessions, Book 8, in substance). Ben Sira’s word is for today.
ch: The Catechism names presumption as a sin against hope: a person either trusts in his own powers to be saved, or presumes on God’s mercy, hoping to be forgiven without conversion (CCC 2092). The Church never preaches less mercy. She preaches mercy received now, in repentance and in the sacrament of Penance, not stored up for later.

set: The teaching in the house at Capernaum goes on. Mark gathers sayings linked partly by key words: “name” (vv. 38–41), “stumble” (vv. 42–47), “fire” and “salt” (vv. 48–50). Such links helped the first Christians to remember Jesus’ words.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts add verses 44 and 46, which repeat verse 48, and add at verse 49 the words “and every sacrifice will be salted with salt” (compare Leviticus 2:13). The NRSV follows the oldest manuscripts and leaves them out, so its numbering skips. Malayalam Bibles number these verses differently.
str: v. 41: a cup of water given because you belong to Christ will be rewarded.
v. 42: woe to whoever makes a little one stumble.
vv. 43–48: hand, foot, eye: cut away what leads to sin.
vv. 49–50: fire and salt; be at peace with one another.
kw: From skandalon, a trap or stumbling block: to make someone fall away from faith or into sin. The verb comes four times in these verses.

Gehenna, the valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem, once a place where children were burned in sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31). It became the name for the final punishment. Verse 48 takes its words from the last verse of Isaiah (66:24).
Literally a “donkey millstone”, the heavy stone turned by an animal, not the small hand mill of a household.
vv: whoever gives you a cup of water to drink because you bear the name of Christ will by no means lose the reward.
The smallest kindness shown to a disciple for Christ’s sake is not forgotten. The outsider of the previous verses is still in view.
If your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off;
This is the strong speech of a prophet, not an order to harm the body. What must be cut away is the habit, the attachment, the occasion that leads us into sin.
Salt is good; but if salt has lost its saltiness, how can you season it? Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another.
Salt preserves and gives taste, and in Leviticus 2:13 it seasons every offering. The section that began with an argument about who was greatest (9:34) ends with peace.
ch: The Church has never read these words as permission to injure the body: the Catechism teaches that mutilation is against the moral law except for strictly therapeutic reasons (CCC 2297). But she takes their seriousness to heart. The Catechism recalls Jesus’ words on Gehenna and the unquenchable fire when it teaches about hell, and calls that teaching an urgent call to conversion (CCC 1034, 1036). Scandal, leading another into sin, is grave, the more so when it harms the weak and the young (CCC 2284–2285).

rite: Today is the optional memorial of St Bernardine of Siena (1380–1444), the Franciscan preacher who carried through the towns of Italy a tablet painted with the letters IHS, the first letters of the name of Jesus in Greek, and spread devotion to the Holy Name. The Gospel fits him well: it begins with a cup of water given “because you bear the name of Christ”.
study: What false confidence (money, strength, or “tomorrow”) keeps me from turning to the Lord today?
What in my life, or in what I let others see, could become a stumbling block for the little ones?
